info.desc: OK Computer is the third album by the English rock band Radiohead, released in 1997. It reached #1 on the UK Albums Chart and marked Radiohead's highest entry into the American market at the time, where it debuted at #21. OK Computer expanded the band's worldwide popularity, becoming the last Radiohead album to have a delayed release outside of the United Kingdom. As of 2007, it has been certified triple platinum in the UK and double platinum in the US. OK Computer included the singles "Paranoid Android", "Karma Police" and "No Surprises". podcast.body: Radiohead's third album, released on July 1, 1997. It became a massively successful and influential album, with its first single "Paranoid Android" reaching number three on the UK singles charts and the album itself hitting number one. The album's title is a reference to a quote from Zaphod Beeblebrox in "The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy" series. There is a theory, based on numbers on the back cover (1857-6397), that the album was finished at 6:57 PM on March 6, 1997. The cover image is an interchange of Interstates 84 and 91, photographed by Tom Yorke from a Hilton Hotel window in Hartford, Connecticut, on August 20, 1996. "A CD called Okay Computing."

podcast.body: Released on July 1, 1997, "OK Computer" stunned critics and fans alike, exceeding high hopes for Radiohead's third album. It was praised for being inventive, subtle, anthemic, adventurous, and rich in moods, textures, sound effects, and brilliant musicianship. The album became the key record of 1997, garnering numerous awards and establishing itself as one of the defining New Rock albums of all time, effectively raising the bar for the subsequent generation of British bands. "It was inventive, and subtle, and anthemic, and adventurous, and full of moods, and textures, and sound effects, and brilliant musicianship."

podcast.body: The album *OK Computer* was predominantly recorded in a unique setting described as a blend of a barn and an old mansion. Its central theme explores the sadness, depression, and loneliness experienced by individuals due to the impact of new technologies and the modern world. Notably, *Exit Music (For a Film)* is one of two tracks on the album whose thematic content deviates from this overarching concept. "The album is dedicated to how people are sad, depressed, and feel alone because of new technologies and the modern world."

podcast.body: The album artwork was designed by Stanley Donwood, who has worked with Radiohead for decades. The front cover is a computer-generated collage in white and various shades of blue, featuring an on-ramp of a motorway, two "lost child" images, a blurred human image, a large black X, and what appears to be the nose of an airplane, designed to present puzzles and mysteries to fans. Fans, after years of research, have identified the primary image as a manipulated photo taken from the window of the Hilton Hotel on August 20, 1996, at the interchange of Interstates 84 and 91 in Hartford, Connecticut, where Radiohead performed at the Meadows Music Theater. This Hartford gig was one of the last before the band returned to the UK to record "OK Computer." The artwork collectively embodies themes of stress in everyday life, commuting, parental concerns, consumerism, and the mundane yet frightening random events of the technological age. "Decoding and deciphering is all part of the fun. After years of research, fans have determined that what we actually see on the cover of OK computer is a manipulated photo taken from the window of the Hilton Hotel on August 20th, 1996, when Radiohead performed at Hartford Connecticut's Meadows Music Theater."

podcast.body: The cover artwork for Radiohead's "OK Computer" depicts an on-ramp to a highway, which was identified by a Reddit user as a real location. It is the eastbound junction of Interstate 84 and Interstate 91 in Hartford, Connecticut, just before the highway crosses the Connecticut River. The photograph was taken from a nearby Hilton hotel window on August 26, 1996, during one of the band's last American shows before recording the album. "Radiohead and Karma Police from OK Computer now cast your imagination to what we see on the front cover of that album."

podcast.body: This album is widely considered one of the most important albums of the 1990s, not just for Radiohead but within the broader music context, noted for its thematic depth and technical recording quality. Despite its critical acclaim, the band, particularly Tom Yorke, expressed a sense of bitterness over its massive commercial success, feeling they had unintentionally created a popular mass-market album instead of the cultural and intellectual work they had intended. This success, however, granted the group complete creative freedom from their record label, which they used to pursue a path of intense experimentation. "tanto por su temática sino técnicamente como está grabado."
